wordings.text: Why do most test suites have many unit tests and few end-to-end tests?
options: Unit tests are fast and point to the part that broke; end-to-end tests are slow and harder to keep stable
End-to-end tests find fewer bugs
Unit tests check the whole system at once
End-to-end tests cannot run automatically

questions.explanation:
Unit tests run in milliseconds and a failure names one function. End-to-end tests check
that the parts work together as a user sees them, but they are slow and depend on many
moving parts, so a few cover the main paths.
questions.summary: Balancing unit, integration and end-to-end tests

wordings.text: Dates are saved with a time zone, but the database column drops it, so times come back shifted. Which is the smallest test that would have caught it?
options: An integration test that saves a date to a real database and reads it back
A unit test of the date code with the database replaced by a fake
An end-to-end test of the whole sign-up flow
A load test

questions.explanation:
The bug is in how two parts meet: the code and the database. A fake database stores
whatever it is given, so the unit test passes. An end-to-end test may catch it, but it
is slower and does not point to the cause.
questions.summary: Which test level catches a bug between two parts

wordings.text: An end-to-end test fails about one run in ten, though nothing has changed. Which are likely causes? Choose all that apply.
options: It waits a fixed time for a page instead of waiting until an element appears
It relies on data that another test leaves behind
It calls a real service that is sometimes slow to answer
The code it tests has a syntax error

questions.explanation:
Flaky tests usually depend on timing, shared state or something outside the test. A
fixed wait is too short when the machine is slow, shared data depends on what ran before,
and a real service answers at its own pace. A syntax error fails every run.

wordings.text: A function accepts ages from 18 to 65, both included. Which inputs test its boundaries?
options: 18 and 65
30 and 50
0 and 100

questions.explanation:
Off-by-one bugs live at the edges: test the last value on each side of each boundary.
18 and 65 alone would miss a check that also accepts 17 or 66.

wordings.text: A function sorts a list of integers, and one test checks `[3, 1, 2]`. Which further cases add the most? Choose all that apply.
options: An empty list
A list with repeated values
A list with negative numbers
`[9, 7, 8]`, another short list in random order

questions.explanation:
Each useful case covers a kind of input the others do not: no elements, equal elements,
values below zero. Another short shuffled list exercises the same paths as the first, so
it is unlikely to find a new bug.
questions.summary: Choosing test cases that cover different kinds of input

wordings.text: A refactoring keeps the behaviour of a module the same but breaks 30 of its tests. What does that suggest?
options: The tests check how the code works, such as which internal calls it makes, rather than what it does
The refactoring must have changed the behaviour
The module needs more tests
The tests should be deleted

questions.explanation:
Tests that check results through the public interface survive a refactoring; that is
their purpose. Tests that check private methods or the order of calls on mocks break
whenever the inside changes, even when nothing is wrong.

wordings.text: A test replaces the email service with an object that records its calls, then checks that `send` was called once, with the user's address. What is this test double called?
options: A mock
A stub
A fake
A dummy

questions.explanation:
A mock checks how it was called. A stub only returns fixed answers, a fake is a simple
working version such as an in-memory database, and a dummy is passed in but never used.

wordings.text: Which of these should a unit test usually replace with a test double? Choose all that apply.
options: A payment provider reached over the network
The current time
A random number generator
A function that adds tax to a price

questions.summary: What to replace in a unit test

wordings.text: A user reports a bug. What should come first?
options: Reproduce it reliably, ideally as a failing test
Change the code that looks most suspicious and see if the bug goes away
Catch the error so the user no longer sees it
Rewrite the module the bug is in

questions.explanation:
A reliable reproduction shows what is wrong and proves when it is fixed; as a test, it
also keeps the bug from coming back. Changes made without one are guesses, and hiding the
error leaves the cause in place.
questions.summary: Starting to debug by reproducing the bug

wordings.text: A bug appeared somewhere in the last 200 commits, and a test shows it. What is the fastest reliable way to find the commit that caused it?
options: Binary search over the commits: about 8 test runs
Test every commit from the newest back: up to 200 runs
Read every change since the last release
Revert all 200 commits

questions.explanation:
Test the commit in the middle: the result shows which half holds the cause. Halving 200
reaches one commit in about log₂ 200 ≈ 8 steps; version control tools can drive this
search, for example `git bisect`.
questions.summary: Finding the commit that caused a bug by binary search
